posts.title: Microsoft CppCon 2026 Trip Report
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
CppCon 2026 is a wrap! Microsoft returned to Aurora, Colorado, for a week of talks, technical discussions, and conversations with developers from across the C++ community.
Microsoft C++ @ CppCon
At our booth, we met people building games, financial systems, developer tools, embedded software, scientific tools, and other applications. Some were working with the latest language features, and others were maintaining and modernizing systems that have been in production for decades. Many talked to us about debugging, performance, build systems, or modern C++, and a growing number were experimenting with ways AI can help them accomplish their goals in the most effective way possible.
Attendees who completed our annual Microsoft C++ survey were entered for our daily LEGO raffle. This year’s prizes included some great LEGO sets; a retro gaming console, a retro camera, a mini orchid, and a model of the Milky Way galaxy.
Congratulations to our raffle winners and thank you to everyone who took the time to share detailed feedback.

Our Talks
I didn’t get a chance to attend many sessions as I spent most of my time talking with folks at the booth, but I was lucky enough to get to see most of our Microsoft sessions as they were being developed.
The Journey to “/W4 /WX”: How Hard Could It Be?

Keith Stockdale, from Rare, presented another session in his series of talks on dealing with the sometimes massive fallout from making small changes to your build system. After first establishing why someone should increase their warning level and treat warnings as errors, Keith walked through the diagnostics that show up, and how they were resolved.
And there were THOUSANDS of warnings, many of them previously suppressed through #pragmas or on the command line. Notably, the one warning that seemed to be the most pervasive was C4189 (local variable is initialized but not referenced) which they took from nearly 10,000 unique warnings down to zero! Definitely check this talk out if you are interested in generally improving the quality of your codebase and keeping your sanity intact while doing so.
C++ in the Age of AI: How Visual Studio Is Evolving

David Li and Augustin Popa presented this year’s version of our “what’s new” session for Visual Studio. GitHub Copilot has become an important part of the modern development toolbox, so much of the session was focused on how those features show up in Visual Studio, including AI workflows to modernize your code, reduce your build times, and debug your projects.
But there were plenty of features and improvements that aren’t specific to AI workflows, as well. Navigating your code in Visual Studio is now much faster with the latest versions, and MSVC Build Tools v14.52 (ships in November, release candidate available now) will ship with all C++23 features implemented and a /std:c++23 switch, which will also be compatible with C++/CLI. The team has also fixed nearly 650 bugs across the compiler, libraries, and IDEs since last year’s conference.
What’s New for C++ in Visual Studio Code: C++ and AI Tooling for Your Build, Your Code, Your Workflow
Watch it on YouTube!

Sinem Akinci and Ben McMorran gave a rundown on the latest and greatest for C++ users of Visual Studio Code. Our Visual Studio Code users are at the forefront of the AI agentic shift, and a lot of this session focused on how you can easily shift between different agentic experiences, depending on the nature of the work, and how you can customize your AI experience with Bring Your Own Key (BYOK), skills, custom agents, and hooks.
I tend to be a Visual Studio guy so a lot of this information wasn’t as useful to me in my day-to-day, but it was nice to see how excited Visual Studio Code users were to talk about their experiences with all of these new features. I for one am looking forward to the day when all AI tools have an easy-to-use BYOK experience that lets you run LLM inference on local hardware.
Turbocharging Native Code Performance: Compiler Optimization, Profile-guided Optimizations, and Beyond

I did get to spend some time in Eric Brumer’s session on how modern CPUs work, how to use profilers, and how those profiles can be used to optimize your products based on behavior of real users. Sample-based Profile Guided Optimizations (SPGO) is a pretty cool evolution of traditional Profile Guided Optimizations (PGO) and it’s already been deployed inside Microsoft to gain non-trivial runtime performance gains.
If you use C++ for the performance it unlocks for your applications, definitely catch this one when it’s available.
The C++ Safety Issues Your Tools Can’t See

Safety for C++ products has been a hot topic over the past decade, and there have been lots of papers and talks on the topic. Ion Todirel’s session starts by summarizing where we have been and introducing a way to discuss the different meanings of safety and how real issues map to them. One of the biggest points that I love to reinforce any chance I get, is that C++ is not C. Many of the problems that C++ has are things that it gets from its history of C compatibility, but unlike C, C++ has a long history of introducing features that are explicitly meant to avoid many of those problems. The talk closes out with a discussion about the broad solution space available to us and how AI can help us make our software safer.
My Major Takeaways
C++ Language Developments
Folks are really excited for new C++ language features, particularly reflection. There were already a couple of sessions, based on existing reflection implementations, showing really compelling things that can be done with the feature. It has the potential to be as impactful as templates were in how we write C++ code.
Performance is King
When we asked developers what they enjoy about C++, they often started with performance and control. CppCon attendees described building low-latency systems, game engines, embedded software, databases, compilers, infrastructure, scientific applications, and other software where memory use, hardware behavior, and predictable performance matter. They value the ability to choose a zero-cost abstraction when one fits, and to choose writing at a lower level when a problem requires it.
AI Normalization
The past few years have seen LLM-based AI workflows become increasingly common for attendees. It feels like there’s been a significant shift in the past year where people have really started to understand how they can use existing AI tools to complete their work faster and easier. Multiple attendees we talked to had conference badges that said something along the line of, “I haven’t written code in N months.” Folks are exploring new product surfaces, such as agentic CLI experiences and mostly-automated agents. There also seems to be much less friction getting started with AI tools, especially as products introduce BYOK capabilities and AI tools get approved for sensitive environments like restricted and air-gapped networks. I expect more talks on how to effectively use AI tools for C++ users in the coming years.
Thank you, CppCon
CppCon is valuable because it brings together people working on very different software who still share many of the same engineering questions.
How can we understand a large codebase more effectively? How can we improve performance without making code harder to maintain? How can we adopt a new language feature safely? Where can AI remove repetitive work, and where does an experienced developer need to stay closely involved?
Thank you to everyone who attended a Microsoft session, visited the booth, completed the survey, participated in an interview, or shared a project with us. Those conversations help us understand your workflows and pain points, and they help us improve the tools you use to make all those awesome products in C++.
CppCon is adding the 2026 session recordings to its video archive on a rolling basis. You can also follow the CppCon YouTube channel and the Microsoft C++ Team Blog for new videos, companion posts, and product updates.
We look forward to continuing the conversation.

posts.title: GenRecs Tokenization: Transforming Ads Recommendation at Meta with Stable Model Vocabulary
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Generative Recommenders (GenRecs) represent a paradigm shift from scoring every ad to reasoning about ad content and user preferences together in order to predict the best outcome for advertisers. Leveraging the world knowledge built into LLMs makes ad matching more intelligent and precise, compounding gains for advertisers.
GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Rather than maintaining a dedicated ID for every item, GenRecs Tokenization represents each item with a set of tokens from a stable semantic vocabulary. 
Paired with Meta’s Generative Ads Model (GEM) and Meta’s Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization has delivered a +0.35% lift in conversions across surfaces for advertisers.
GenRecs improves the way Meta’s ads recommendation systems make predictions today. Short for Generative Recommenders, GenRecs shifts our approach from scoring every individual ad candidate to leveraging LLM architecture to deeply reason about ad content and user preferences simultaneously. By pairing pre-trained world knowledge with a semantic understanding of what an ad actually represents, the system moves beyond click-pattern matching to understand underlying user preferences. This allows the model to predict the most relevant ad for each person, even when surfacing brand-new products with no past product, ad or company engagement history. 
GenRecs Tokenization is the foundational data representation that makes this possible. Instead of maintaining a dedicated ID for every concept in the world, language models compose a small vocabulary of semantic tokens to represent any concept. Because tokens describe what an item (e.g., ads, products, services, etc.) is, the model can relate an item it has never seen engagement for, to items it knows well. A newly launched “trail shoe” inherits what the model has already learned about that category, rather than starting a new representation with no signal.
GenRecs Tokenization introduces a structured vocabulary approach for ad recommendations, enabling GenRecs for both retrieval and ranking across every item type in the system, including ads, products, pages, and pixels. 

Meta’s state-of-the-art ads recommendation system drives ongoing advertiser performance improvements by learning about individual items and how they perform . LLMs present a unique opportunity to further improve the performance of recommendation systems by leveraging semantic tokenization in several ads use cases:
Accelerating learning from new entities: Semantic tokenization helps models to infer relevance and establish relationships through shared concepts. New entities include newly created ads, niche products, and pages with limited engagement.
Enabling cross-campaign transfer: Semantic tokenization creates a stable vocabulary that allows the models to carry insights across campaigns for advertisers.
LLM scaling benefits: Semantic tokenization allows the benefits to compound with the LLM scaling curve’s improving performance. 
Infusing world knowledge: Semantic tokenization gives pre-trained language models a direct interface to reason about ad content and user intent.
Once items are migrated to semantic tokens, models learn from token patterns much like LLMs do. In production, this yields:
Prediction accuracy improvements in production: Paired with Meta’s GEM and Adaptive Ranking Model, GenRecs Tokenization delivered a +0.35% lift1 in conversions.
Compounding feedback loop: Better tail predictions yield better lessons from tail ads which enrich the training data to further improve predictions for all ads from the model, creating a performance improving feedback loop. 
A new way to scale: Across production ranking and retrieval, tokens bend the scaling curve along sequence length, training data, and model architecture.
1 Meta Internal Data, measured in February 2026.
Introducing GenRecs Tokenization
Pre-trained multimodal models read each ad, product, and page, including its text and images, and encode the items into an embedding that carries world knowledge. The tokenizer combines that content signal with representations learned from how people engage with the items, then quantizes the result into a short sequence of discrete tokens. Similar items share tokens, much as related words share roots. For example, there’s overlap between two running shoe ads from the previous season to the current season, so the new campaign immediately benefits from everything the model has already learned about the previous season’s products.
At the heart of GenRecs Tokenization is a three-stage pipeline that: 
Encodes each item into a semantic embedding space.
Decomposes that embedding into independent subspaces.
Quantizes by mapping each subspace to an entry in a codebook. 

Maximizing ads recommendation quality requires diverse combinations of these stages depending on entity and feature semantics. For example, for many ad representations, GenRecs Tokenization uses prefix n-grams that combine a learned encoder, residual decomposition,  learned vector codebooks, and token parametrization. 
Token Quality Predicts Ranking Accuracy
Independently of downstream ranking gain, tokenizer model quality can be evaluated against intrinsic measures like:
Cluster purity: The items that share a code tend to share a category, giving the model a cleaner signal per token;
Distribution balance: Items spread evenly across semantic IDs instead of crowding into a few.
Codebook utilization: A larger share of codes holds at least one item, so the vocabulary expresses more distinctions.
Across the eight tokenizer versions we tested, we see a strong correlation between these intrinsic quality metrics and downstream ranking prediction accuracy. Tokenizer versions that scored better on these metrics also had better CTR prediction accuracy for ads models.

The Tokenization Flywheel
Tokenization maximizes the efficiency of high-volume campaigns by uncovering deeper semantic patterns across their vast product catalogs. For tail ads that accumulate fewer impressions, tokenization enables ads recommendation models to generalize across them via shared content structure, recovering cold-start performance and enabling cross-entity transfer. When a sportswear brand launches next season’s trail shoe, tokenization lets the new product and its ads build on what the model learned from last season’s shoe, even before anyone sees the new ad.
By improving tail ad prediction quality, tokenization not only lets tail ads be ranked accurately, but also improves the training data, which then improves prediction quality for all ads. Each pass through this self-reinforcing flywheel improves the quality of model predictions.
 
The Foundations of LLM Recommendation
Tokenizer improvements are not confined to the model they were tuned for. Optimizing codebook quality through diversity loss, dead code resets, and contrastive objectives produces measurably better downstream performance when the resulting tokens train generative recommenders. Our work on LLM-native retrieval shows how far this can go. A two-tower architecture built on a shared LLM encoder reaches state-of-the-art retrieval quality while remaining efficiently servable, matching classic two-tower performance on a fraction of the training data. Building on this, we are now extending reasoning-aware ranking on top of the same vocabulary.
The Future of GenRecs Tokenization
We are continuing to push GenRecs Tokenization toward the ROI-optimal frontier along three directions:
Deepening cold-start generalization: Tail ad inventory is where semantic tokens contribute most and where advertiser impact is largest. We are scaling the coverage of tokenization across all items to deliver better performance to advertisers.
Treating tokenizer quality as a first-class objective: Engagement-aligned training, unified cross-entity vocabulary, and codebook improvements are active areas of investment. Because intrinsic quality measures predict downstream ranking gains, we can iterate on the tokenizer without waiting on a full model training cycle.
Serving LLM-native architectures efficiently: Fully verbalized tokenization gives a model the richest view of an ad, but requires context windows that are impractical at ads scale. We are combining compacted verbalized tokens with semantic IDs to retain reasoning quality while maintaining acceptable latency.
Looking further out, we are exploring whether the same vocabulary that improves ads ranking today could unify representation across surfaces. A shared token space spanning ads content across text, image, audio, and video, would let models reason about what a person is interested in and what an advertiser has to offer with one representation, rather than stitching together separately learned embeddings. 
As recommendation systems evolve from discriminative scoring to include generative reasoning, the data foundation benefits from evolving from ephemeral IDs to stable semantic representations. GenRecs Tokenization provides the foundation, translating the complexity of Meta’s ads ecosystem into a vocabulary that generative models can learn, reason about, and generate from.
Acknowledgements
We would like to thank Weifeng Cui, Ling Leng, Luke Simon, Hadar Ohana, Jimmy Chen, Minghai Chen, Chiyu Zhang, Dinesh Ramasamy, Debajyoti Roy, Shawn Shi, Gajanan Golegaonkar, Xiao Yang, Ashkan Aleali, Anuj Gargava, Xizhou Feng, Liquan Huang, Frank Shyu, Xiaoyu Chen, Kungang Li, Chonglin Sun, Matt Steiner, Sandeep Pandey,  Santanu Kolay, Anuj Madan, Tak Yan, and the entire team behind the development and productionization of the first large scale semantic tokenization effort in Meta’s ad recommendation system.

posts.title: The Thin Orchestrator: How We Made Our AI Agents More Reliable by Giving the Router Less to Do
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
Sometimes, giving an AI agent all of the knowledge it needs is the wrong approach. 
At Meta, we’ve seen notable improvements in efficiency and accuracy by keeping the orchestration layer of our data pipeline agents deliberately thin: It routes work and enforces reliability checks, while specialized agents do the domain reasoning.
We’re sharing our own process and insights, plus how any team can apply this to their production AI agents.
We built a 1,300-line orchestrator that routes 20+ workflows to 14 specialized AI agents. It performs zero domain work itself. That’s the point.
When we first deployed AI agents to automate data column onboarding across Meta’s recommendation systems — a process spanning three code repositories, three programming languages, and up to six pipeline stages that must stay in sync — we did what most teams do: We built one smart agent that knew everything.
It worked in demos. In production, it started hallucinating.
The fix wasn’t better prompts or a bigger context window. It was giving the central agent less to do. We call this the thin orchestrator pattern: a router that owns sequencing and reliability checks, and leaves every domain decision to specialists.
The Problem: More Context, Worse Results
Our pipeline is config-as-code: Python configurations drive C++ code generation, which feeds data processing services, which populate analytics systems. Onboarding a single data column requires coordinated changes across configuration registries, backend services, and data pipelines, and each column moves through up to six stages before its data arrives.
Our first approach was a single AI agent loaded with all domain knowledge, configuration schemas, code generation rules, pipeline routing logic, validation requirements, and population patterns for 10+ data sources. 
The agent had everything it needed. That was the problem.
Past a certain context threshold, additional knowledge degraded rather than improved performance. The agent would cross-contaminate concepts, applying field naming conventions from one subsystem to another, or using a code generation pattern meant for one data source when populating from a different one. A preprint from the Windreich Department of Artificial Intelligence and Human Health at Mount Sinai found that orchestrated multiagent systems held 65.3% accuracy at 80-task batches where single agents fell to 16.6%, while reducing token usage up to 65-fold. The authors attribute this to the design’s isolation of tasks, which prevented context interference. We were experiencing the inverse, a single agent drowning in its own knowledge.
We also evaluated an alternative single-agent approach. Its success rate was 70-80% with manual prompt engineering per task: An engineer had to craft a custom system prompt for each specific job. Without that handholding, success dropped to 10-20%. This wasn’t a prompt engineering problem. It was an architectural one.
The Approach: A Thin Router With Specialist Workers
We split the system into two layers:
A deterministic orchestrator that performs zero domain work. It classifies intent, gathers required fields, runs reliability checks, and delegates to the right specialist. It never reasons about code, never generates configurations, and never touches the codebase. It’s a router.
Fourteen specialized subagents, each a complete domain expert with isolated context. A schema management agent knows configuration registries. A population agent knows how to generate code for each of 10 data sources. A validation agent knows build systems and quality checks. No agent sees the full picture. That’s the feature, not the bug.
The orchestrator follows a fixed 7-step protocol for every request:
Read the relevant subagent’s instruction file.
Check if the target already exists (prevent duplicates).
Gather required fields from the user.
Auto-discover what can be inferred (repository type, existing configurations).
Reliability gate check for active warnings or required reviewers.
Delegate to the subagent with full context.
Handle results and surface errors, confirm success.
Steps 1–5 and 7 are deterministic. Only step 6 involves large language model (LLM) reasoning, and it happens inside an isolated subagent with only its domain knowledge loaded.
What We Built: Workflow Templates, Not New Agents

One architectural insight was separating what needs to happen from how each step is performed. The orchestrator defines phase ordering through workflow templates — deterministic state machines that constrain the LLM’s decision space:
Column Onboarding: Schema → Validation → Population → Testing
Event Onboarding: Schema → Population → Validation → Testing → Event Processing
Pipeline Migration: Assessment → Planning → Population → Validation → Monitoring
Each workflow template reuses the same pool of 14 subagents in different sequences. When we needed to support pipeline migration, a completely new use case, we didn’t build new agents. We wrote a new workflow template that sequenced existing agents differently. Zero new agent code. Full production capability.
Each subagent follows a standardized structure:
Knowledge sources: which domain files to load at runtime (typically a few thousand tokens each).
Pre-gathering checklist: what the orchestrator must collect before delegation.
Step-by-step workflow: the domain-specific execution plan.
Discovery patterns: how to find relevant code patterns in the monorepo.
Troubleshooting: error-to-resolution mappings for common failures.
This uniformity means adding a new subagent is templated work, not greenfield engineering. The 15th subagent looks structurally identical to the first.
Knowledge files are loaded on demand at subagent execution time, not embedded in the orchestrator. We maintain 25+ knowledge files organized by workflow domain. When a knowledge file is updated, the next session automatically uses the latest version — no orchestrator changes required. The same knowledge files serve multiple platform implementations of our agent.
Results
Configuration prep for a new column took three to four days by hand and about a day with our earlier config-driven system. The thin orchestrator system does it in under an hour.
For broader context: About two-thirds of the system’s changes land without significant human edits. It gets there by trading generality for deep domain knowledge, a deliberate architectural choice. The orchestrator is general; the subagents are specialists.
Why This Works (And Why Heavyweight Orchestrators Don’t)
The conventional approach is to make the orchestrator the smartest component — give it all the context and let it reason about what to do and how to do it. This works until it doesn’t, and it stops working exactly when you need it most — at scale, with complex multi-step workflows, across heterogeneous subsystems.
The thin orchestrator works because it aligns architectural boundaries with computational boundaries:
Deterministic decisions stay deterministic. “Which subagent handles this?” is a routing decision, not a reasoning task. Don’t use an LLM for it.
Context isolation prevents cross-contamination. The population agent for data source A never sees data source B’s patterns. It can’t hallucinate the wrong one.
Failures are contained. If a subagent fails, the orchestrator retries or escalates. The failure doesn’t corrupt the orchestrator’s state or other subagents’ contexts.
The system improves at every layer independently. A better model improves all 14 subagents simultaneously. A knowledge file update takes effect immediately. A new workflow template unlocks new capabilities without touching agents. No single component carries the full weight.
How to Apply This to Your AI Agents
This pattern isn’t specific to data pipelines. Any team building production AI agents can benefit:
 Separate routing from reasoning. If your orchestrator is making domain decisions, it’s doing too much. Routing should be deterministic: keyword matching, intent classification, field gathering. Push all domain reasoning into isolated subagents.
 Design subagents as structurally uniform specialists. Every subagent should have the same structure: knowledge sources, required inputs, execution steps, error handling. This makes adding new capabilities templated work rather than architecture changes.
 Use workflow templates, not new agents, to scale. When you need a new use case, first ask: Can I sequence existing agents differently? If you can’t reuse agents across workflows, your agents are too coupled to specific use cases.
 Load knowledge at runtime, not at build time. Embed knowledge in the orchestrator and every update requires redeployment. Load it on demand and updates take effect immediately, across all platforms.
 Draw the deterministic/probabilistic boundary explicitly. For every component, decide: Is this a routing decision (deterministic) or a reasoning task (probabilistic)? The orchestrator should be on one side, the subagents on the other. Don’t mix them.
The strongest argument for a thin orchestrator is the failure mode of the alternative. When a heavyweight orchestrator hallucinates, the error spreads to everything downstream: it routes to the wrong agent, gathers the wrong fields, or skips reliability checks. A thin orchestrator leaves little room for hallucination because its routing and reliability steps don’t rely on LLM reasoning. It follows a fixed protocol. The creativity happens downstream, in isolated, domain-scoped contexts where hallucination risk is minimized and failures are contained.
What’s Next
We’re scaling this architecture to handle an increase in data columns across new pipeline domains. The compositional thesis predicts this will work because scaling means adding workflow templates and knowledge files, not rebuilding agents. We’re also exploring how the system can continuously improve from production usage, using automated feedback loops to identify failure patterns and propose targeted improvements to subagent knowledge, with human review always gating any changes.
The counterintuitive lesson: the most important component in our AI agent system is the one that does the least work. Keep your orchestrator thin and your specialists deep, and the whole system becomes more reliable.
Acknowledgements
This work was a team effort. Some other people who contributed to this effort include:  Mani Bhushan, Rahul Maliakkal, Jae Ha, Chakrapani Kumar, Vivek Tiwari, and Amanda Yin.

posts.title: Inside Prometheus: Meta’s Journey to a Gigawatt-Scale Supercluster
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
With the recent release of the Muse family of foundational models, we want to take you inside the infrastructure that has made it all possible.
The first phase of Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is already complete and we’re working toward scaling it to comprise  ~1 million GPUs.
Prometheus also features technologies like closed-loop liquid cooling to help it operate efficiently.
Right now, in New Albany, Ohio, Meta is undertaking its most ambitious AI infrastructure project to date. Prometheus, our gigawatt-scale supercluster, is an advancement in our infrastructure that is training the next generation of foundational models that will bring new AI experiences to billions of people.
Two years ago, New Albany was a conventional data center site running web traffic. With advancements in hardware, networking and building design, we reworked this site to be home to training programs for frontier models. We’re building the supercluster in phases. The first phase has already been completed and was used to train our Muse foundational models, including the Muse Wonder models, our new frontier models that deliver state-of-the-art performance on personal and professional agentic tasks. 
Large training jobs require everything to work optimally to sustain their performance; an issue on a single host can slow down or stop the entire job, lowering its ‘goodput’. By focusing on improving our systems’ stability and reliability we were able to achieve more than 85% goodput for pre-training runs and more than 90% goodput for reinforcement learning (RL) runs of Muse Wonder. During these training runs, we were able to achieve an overall wall-clock mean time between interruptions (MTBI) of ~47k GPU hours. Since then, we have landed further changes across our fleet including firmware fixes to increase MTBI to more than 54K GPU hours, and we are constantly improving it.
Now, we’re continuing to scale Prometheus with our next frontier models from Meta Superintelligence Labs in mind.
https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_Video_v1.mp4
The Prometheus supercluster is housed in Meta’s New Albany, Ohio, data center.
The Supercluster: Unlocking New AI Capabilities
Today, Prometheus comprises an array of hundreds of thousands of GPUs across multiple interconnected buildings, including traditional and AI-optimized data center buildings and rapid deployment structures, all tightly interconnected by miles of fiber and functioning as a single machine. 
This capacity allows us to pursue larger models and longer context windows than were previously practical. At full scale, Prometheus will comprise roughly 1 million distributed GPUs, all functioning in lockstep. 
Multiple Generations of AI Hardware
Prometheus currently deploys two NVIDIA GPU platforms, with a third (based on NVIDIA’s Vera Rubin NVL72) arriving soon. Each represents a generational leap in performance and efficiency, leveraging our NVL72 rack architecture where 72 GPUs act as a single accelerator within the same network fabric.
Catalina: NVIDIA GB200
Our first platform, Catalina, leverages the NVIDIA GB200 NVL72. We deploy the Ariel variant, a two-rack configuration in which 36 GPUs per rack are interconnected via NVLink to form a unified 72-GPU domain. Catalina provides improvements in raw compute and memory capacity compared to Grand Teton H100. It leverages our Open Rack V3 (ORv3) high-power rack (HPR) structure, an open hardware design contributed to the Open Compute Project (OCP). 
The Ariel variant of GB200 NVL72 pairs each NVIDIA Blackwell GPU with an NVIDIA Grace CPU and 2x NVIDIA ConnectX-7 400G NICs at a 1:1 CPU-to-GPU ratio, letting us deploy 800G of I/O per GPU earlier than the rest of the industry. We chose Ariel because the GB200 NVL72 scaled up nearly every other dimension relative to the NVIDIA H100: FLOPS, HBM bandwidth, scale-up bandwidth, and scale-up domain size, while scale-out bandwidth per GPU would have stayed at 400G. We expected that imbalance to cost performance, so we opted for a configuration that delivers 800G of scale-out per GPU. This also gave us more uniformity of spec as the region expanded over time and 800G scale-out became available.
https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_GB200_GIF_v1.mp4


72 NVIDIA Blackwell GPUs with 13.4 TB of HBM3e (192 GB per GPU).
720 peak PFLOPS of FP8 training compute (1,440 PFLOPS at FP4).
130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth within the domain.
576 TB/s peak aggregate memory bandwidth.
~120 kW total system power across the two-rack pair.
Clemente: NVIDIA GB300 NVL72
Our second platform, Clemente, moves to the NVIDIA GB300 NVL72 and improves on Catalina at both the GPU and the platform level. GB300 raises HBM capacity per GPU by 1.5x, from 192 GB to 288 GB, and dense FP4 throughput by a similar factor, while roughly doubling attention (softmax) acceleration. At the platform level, scale-out is no longer the constraint it was on the GB200 NVL72: NVIDIA ConnectX-8 SuperNICs deliver 800G per GPU natively, so the capability we deployed early on Ariel becomes the baseline. That, together with a 2:1 GPU-to-CPU ratio, allows Clemente to pack the full 72-GPU domain into a single rack, streamlining our physical deployment. Clemente can be deployed with our modular Air-Assisted Liquid Cooling (AALC) or use Facility Liquid Cooling (FLC) in our newly designed data centers. Serviceability also improves substantially, with reduced cabling.
https://engineering.fb.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/AIM-1210-Superclusters_GB300_GIF_v1.mp4
The Clemente GB300 NVL72 features:
72 NVIDIA Blackwell Ultra GPUs with 20.7 TB of HBM3e (288 GB per GPU — 50% more than the GB200).
Over 1 exaFLOP of peak FP4 compute.
130 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth (1.8 TB/s bidirectional per GPU).
~135 kW rack power.
5-10% performance improvement over the GB200 NVL72.
Connecting the Supercluster
In traditional web services, the data center network transports requests and responses between services whose instances typically don’t require high bandwidth, high performance, and tight, lock-step coordination across many servers. Large-scale AI training requires all these, meaning the network that connects them is now an important part of AI workloads. To best address this, in addition to the standard data center network connecting servers, several years ago we added a second dedicated data network based on Ethernet, called the Back-End (BE) network, to enable direct GPU-to-GPU communication both within and across data center buildings.
Large pre-training jobs partition the training into data-parallel model replicas, creating a hierarchy in network usage: Latency-sensitive and bandwidth-sensitive operations concentrate within a replica, while traffic that is more tolerant of higher latency and less bandwidth is scheduled between replicas. Our network is designed to match this hierarchy, with low-latency, high-bandwidth fabrics within buildings and an aggregation network connecting the building fabrics. 
We work closely with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure the parallelism design, traffic patterns, and communication algorithms and software are optimized to minimize exposure of any network communication. This keeps the GPUs as busy as possible and not waiting on the network.
The Meta team has employed these networking concepts in earlier building-scale, 24K GPU clusters and our region-scale, 100K+ GPU cluster over the last several years, and we took them to a new level of scale and distance in Prometheus.
Network Fabrics
At the building level, each Ethernet-based fabric interconnects up to 20,736 GPUs through a high-bandwidth, low-latency multi-layer topology. Our initial design used a Disaggregated Scheduled Fabric (DSF) to mitigate the network congestion caused by training collectives that typically have a small number of large, long-lived network flows that collide under traditional load-balancing techniques; it does this by utilizing sub-packet-level multipath routing and packet re-ordering in the fabric along with virtual output queues and credit-based end-to-end flow control. 
As Ethernet NIC technology advanced, enabling packet re-ordering at the endpoint, we were able to update to a Non-Scheduled Fabric (NSF) utilizing shallow-buffer 51.2T Ethernet switches, such as Minipack3 with Dynamic Load Balancing and the NVIDIA Spectrum-4 switch ASIC-based Minipack3N with NVIDIA’s Adaptive Routing on ConnectX NICs. Both DSF and NSF are based on Meta’s FBOSS networking stack, giving us the control to rapidly iterate on and optimize the fabrics in Prometheus, and the visibility to operate these clusters at scale.
Aggregation
The Backend Aggregation (BAG) network is a multi-layer hub-and-spoke network that connects building-level fabrics across the Prometheus cluster, spanning 2 km to over 100 km. It is built with Arista 7800-series chassis running deep-buffered Broadcom Jericho3 silicon, delivering multiple Pbps of bandwidth per region pair. 

Running pretraining over this network required a dedicated optimization effort with Meta Superintelligence Labs to ensure training was not slowed down, especially given speed-of-light constraints at these distances.

Pulling this all together, the complexity of the Prometheus network involves millions of miles of fiber strand, tens of thousands of switches, and millions of optics — from 2×400G FR4 LITE short-reach, low-cost pluggables inside the buildings to 800G-ZR coherent optics for links beyond ~10 km.

Engineering Reliability at Every Level
At Prometheus’ scale, every component needs to be monitored for reliability. A single fault anywhere can halt an entire training job and waste valuable compute resources. 
Maintaining reliability at this level requires a co-engineering model with NVIDIA that goes beyond a traditional vendor dynamic. Teams are deeply embedded at our data centers, sharing real-time telemetry and running joint triage sessions to decompose every system halt by its root cause.
This attribution-driven accountability model ensures both sides are focused on targeted improvements. While Meta optimizes scheduling and infrastructure, NVIDIA addresses firmware, signal diagnostics, and memory handling. This transparency eliminates ambiguity and drives faster fixes across both organizations.
The 72-GPU Failure Domain
The transition from the H100 generation’s NVL8 architecture to NVL72 has fundamentally redefined our approach to infrastructure resilience. In the NVL8 era, the scale-up domain — the group of GPUs tightly coupled via NVLink for tensor parallelism — was limited to eight units. With NVL72, that domain expands to 72 GPUs, increasing the fault blast radius by 9X.
The larger scale-up domain is what gives NVL72 its bandwidth advantage, but it also makes the 72-GPU rack the unit of allocation we plan capacity around. Training parallelism maps most efficiently onto power-of-two group sizes, so each NVL72 domain runs a 64-GPU slice and keeps its remaining eight GPUs as in-rack spares. When a GPU fails, a spare takes its place immediately, so the job restarts from its last checkpoint instead of waiting on hardware repair, and the rack stays in the job. The in-rack redundancy pushes the effective rack fault rate down to the floor set by failures that can remove an entire pod; for rarer whole-rack faults we hold roughly 2% additional racks in reserve. For a 32,768 active-GPU training run, this means provisioning 523 NVL72 racks, or 37,656 GPUs, about 13% above the active footprint. Most of that margin (11%) falls out of the 64-of-72 slice geometry rather than being an absolute reliability tax.
Physical complexity further intensifies these reliability requirements. A single NVL72 domain incorporates 5,184 tuned differential-pair signaling links operating at 200 Gbps, each traversing multiple potential points of failure, including GPU SerDes, compute tray PCBs, cable cartridges, and switch tray interfaces. Maintaining consistent signal integrity across this dense fabric — at 200 Gbps per lane — represents an unprecedented engineering challenge at this scale.
Fault Recovery 
Fault recovery addresses how we react to faults to minimize the impact on training time. Depending on the scope (i.e., blast area) of a fault we address it through two mechanisms:
Parallelism-Aware Fault Tolerance (PAFT): When a fault can be isolated to a data-parallel model replica, we reduce the impact of a hardware failure by allowing a single faulty replica to be taken offline, while the remaining cluster repeats that step and continues productive training. The compromised slice simply restarts on available spare hosts and resynchronizes, converting a potential total system halt into a minor, temporary reduction in aggregate throughput.
Checkpointing: When a fault blast area is larger than a data-parallel model replica, the entire job is restarted back to the last checkpoint; frequent checkpointing reduces the amount of work lost in these events. Our distributed checkpointing architecture asynchronously saves the model state — including gradients and optimizer data — to multi-tier storage. We use delta checkpointing and in-memory staging to ensure these saves happen with minimal impact on training throughput.
These two fault recovery mechanisms combine with a sparing strategy that utilizes pre-allocated spare GPU trays within a rack, as well as spare racks, to minimize the time to bring up replacement hardware and reduce the amount of work lost to hardware failures
Systematic Reduction of Interruptions
When training frontier models, infrastructure reliability requires a perspective beyond simple availability. The fundamental challenge lies in maintaining training momentum without frequent system halts. Within Prometheus, we classify an interruption as any fault — from GPU silicon defects and network fabric anomalies to storage bottlenecks or thermal limits — that forces a job to pause and initiate a recovery cycle.
These interruptions introduce a large operational overhead because our workloads are tightly interdependent; a single fault within a 72-GPU domain can affect the entire cluster’s aggregate throughput. This performance loss directly impacts our engineering iteration speed, resulting in less effective compute and longer timelines for delivering advanced AI experiences to billions of people.

During the initial phase of Prometheus in mid-2025, our interruption rates reached a peak of nearly 1,000 events per 8K GPUs daily. Through a year of rigorous cross-functional engineering, we have achieved a 99% reduction in interruptions, enabling the cluster to sustain multiple training jobs of tens of thousands of GPUs in parallel.
Attaining this stability required a granular decomposition of every interruption source, followed by the deployment of targeted engineering solutions for each failure category:
NVLink Signal Integrity: initially the primary bottleneck for GB200 deployments. With over 600,000 NVLink connections, even marginal signal degradation triggers frequent NVLink recovery cycles. We implemented continuous telemetry and automated flagging, utilizing L11 diagnostic burns to isolate weak links before production. Our classification tools distinguish transient faults from persistent signal integrity failures, guiding targeted repairs and component replacement, and we validate repaired systems before returning them to production. 
Memory Reliability (HBM and LPDDR): Memory-related faults became a major source of interruptions as we scaled GB300 with higher memory capacities. Working closely with NVIDIA, we used fleet telemetry and detailed error analysis to identify recurring failure signatures, which are mitigated via refined HBM firmware settings, memory scrubbing, an improved error correction algorithm for LPDDR, and pattern-based predictive detection to retire degrading devices before they impact job throughput. We are deploying these changes across the fleet and measuring their impact on interruption rates and hardware replacement demand.
NVLink Switch and Fabric Health: A single switch fault can compromise an entire NVL72 domain. We monitor fabric health at millisecond resolution, utilizing automated recovery paths to isolate faulty components and rebalance traffic across the remaining infrastructure without a job interruption.
Backend Network Events: At the BAG super-spine layer, link events are managed transparently via hardware-based fault detection. Our planar topologies ensure that individual fiber or port failures are rerouted without interrupting the synchronized GPU traffic bursts.
Sustained improvement is driven by our operational infrastructure: A colocated triage team at the New Albany site, a comprehensive stability sprint in March that synchronized fixes across the stack, and a rigorous attribution-driven accountability framework. Every repair undergoes a mandatory quarantine to validate system integrity before returning to the compute pool.
Our reliability north star remains two interruptions per 8K GPUs per day, which is ~100k GPU hours MTBI. Driving a 99% reduction from our peak interruptions rate demonstrates that, at Prometheus’ scale, stability is an engineering challenge with solvable engineering outcomes.
Maturing Hardware at Fleet Scale
Deploying hundreds of thousands of first-generation accelerators reveals quality issues that are hidden at lower volumes. The GB200 deployment has transformed hardware maturation into a primary engineering discipline for our teams and partners.
Areas of engineering include:
Rapid Firmware Bundle Deployment: We built reliable and fast firmware bundle automation, capable of deploying firmware and driver fixes to more than 100k GPUs within a few hours. We’ve brought down the P90 of single-pod upgrade times from more than seven hours in early hardware introduction to two hours. This has let us push rapid fixes for the top interruption categories to our fleet.
Fleet Health: We correlate telemetry across multi-rack systems and classify every job interruption to guide software fixes, hardware repairs, and replacement decisions. We track MTBI alongside available capacity plus effective training throughput, and have a robust feedback cycle for hardware and software reliability improvements to translate into more productive compute. 
Cross-Partner Qualification: implementing parallel validation with multiple manufacturing partners to ensure consistent quality through continuous feedback from our production fleet.
Automated Signal Screening: validating over 600,000 NVLink paths using diagnostic stress tests before any production traffic is routed. Even minor defect rates at this scale require proactive identification.
Power Delivery Stress Testing: investigating how PSU modules and voltage regulators interact under the 1,400W load of individual GPUs to surface failure modes that only appear at high volumes.
Precision Liquid Cooling: enforcing strict quality gates for cold plate and manifold assembly to maintain optimal junction temperatures and prevent leaks across the fleet.
Fleet Maintenance: proactive preparation, rapid disposition, prioritization for fix-repair, and prepositioning spares. 
Health Checks: advanced ingestion/burn-in and pre-job health checks used to identify healthy nodes for inclusion in large training jobs.
Each new platform architecture — from Blackwell to Vera Rubin — incorporates these real-world operational insights, tightening our screening and design specifications at every step.
Optimizing Power and Managing Transients
Maximizing throughput for a given power envelope, minimizing stranded power, and synchronous distributed training introduces a power delivery hurdle. When tens of thousands of GPUs execute compute-heavy phases and communication cycles in unison, they trigger large power transients — sudden load fluctuations of 30-40% within the cluster. Initiating or pausing a major training job can shift loads of more than tens of megawatts in just seconds.
We address this with Dynamo Dimmer, our cluster-wide power management framework that enables intelligent power capping. Instead of hard-stopping workloads, Dimmer gradually adjusts GPU power limits as the cluster nears its electrical ceiling, ensuring training continues uninterrupted. This system is reinforced by rack-level battery backup (BBU) modules that handle immediate spikes, capacitor trays (CBUs) for peak smoothing, facility-level battery energy storage systems (BESS), and deep coordination with utility providers to manage these unique AI profiles. 
Managing Cooling in a Heterogenous Fleet
While our distributed approach has allowed us to build Prometheus quickly, it has also meant navigating site-specific power and cooling constraints across different locations. 
Our physical infrastructure incorporates multiple cooling generations to deliver the liquid cooling required by these high-power racks. Prometheus runs on a mix of modular air-assisted liquid cooling (AALC), including our free-air data center buildings and our rapid-deployment structures. Our purpose-built AI-optimized building now uses facility liquid cooling (FLC) for maximum power density. 
By integrating leased capacity from strategic partners in addition to our own buildings, we accelerate our deployment timelines and total deployable capacity. Meanwhile, our industrial-grade rapid-deployment structures have redefined the construction playbook, delivering production-ready compute with faster timelines.
Operating Efficiently 
In New Albany, we’ve long partnered with local utilities to ensure we are paying the full cost of energy for our site and not adding any unnecessary strain to the local grid. We’ve also partnered with energy developers to match our energy use with new clean and renewable energy. 
Meta’s newest AI-optimized data centers use closed-looped, liquid cooling as it is the most efficient way to cool GPU servers, and supports efficient use of water. Direct-to-chip, closed-loop liquid cooling helps save space by allowing us to fit more GPUs on a server rack. We also work to extend our sustainability work by sharing designs for systems like IcePack, our liquid-cooled network rack, with the wider industry through OCP.
Beyond Prometheus
We’ll continue to work closely with NVIDIA to expand Prometheus’ capacity with a mix of NVIDIA GB300 NVL72s and NVIDIA Vera Rubin NVL72s.
NVIDIA’s next-generation Vera Rubin NVL72 platform will be a generational leap in per-GPU performance and will integrate directly into Prometheus’s existing network fabric. As the cluster matures, it will deliver even more compute per watt by augmenting its capacity (primarily interconnected GB300s) with Vera Rubin via our upcoming San Miguel platform.


The San Miguel Vera Rubin NVL72 will feature:
72 NVIDIA Vera Rubin GPUs with 288 GB of HBM4 and 19.2 TB/s peak bandwidth per GPU.
2.52 peak EFLOPS of FP4 training compute 1.26 peak EFLOPS FP8 training per rack.
216 TB/s peak NVLink bandwidth (3 TB/s bidirectional per GPU).
~1,500 TB/s peak aggregate memory bandwidth.
Fully liquid-cooled compute trays at over 170 kW per rack.
10-20% improvement in performance per watt over the GB300 NVL72.
The technological accomplishments within Prometheus have helped establish the blueprint that will inform how we approach the complexity of supercluster design going forward. Hyperion, our upcoming supercluster in Richland Parish, Louisiana, is being designed from the ground up with insights from Prometheus in mind. It will feature closed-loop liquid cooling, full grid connectivity with our utility partner Entergy, for which Meta pays the full cost, and next-generation network designs. 
Learn more about our community efforts in New Albany.

posts.title: Beyond API Compatibility: Building a Tool to Measure the Blast Radius of Library Changes
posts.content:encodedSnippet:
By Roberto Perez Alcolea, Java Platform Team
Quasar connects a proposed API change with observed references in consumer repositories, giving the producer evidence for a release decision
At Netflix, shared Java libraries support applications developed across a large, independently evolving repository ecosystem. A library change begins in one repository, but its impact can reach many others. Producers can see the API diff in front of them. What they often cannot see is who still depends on the symbols that changed.
The need for that visibility grows as coding agents take on more of the software development lifecycle. An agent can accelerate a local edit, but without cross-repository context it cannot judge downstream risk or help plan consumer migrations. The evidence a producer uses to assess a change can also guide the agent working on it.
Consider a common case: removing a deprecated API. Deprecated entry points expand the surface producers must test, document, and support, and they can constrain how a library evolves.
Suppose a replacement has been available for several releases and the old method cannot express options required by new behavior. The library’s tests pass, and a compatibility checker flags the removal. The producer still cannot answer the questions that determine what to do next:

Does any consumer still call this method?
Are consumers concentrated on one version or spread across several generations?
Does another library implement or wrap the API, multiplying its impact?
Is direct coordination sufficient, or does this require a deprecation and migration campaign?

At small scale, producers can ask nearby teams or search a handful of repositories. Across many repositories, it is harder to find every caller of a method and the library version each one uses. Those answers are scattered across consumer codebases and builds.
Without that evidence, a producer may release a breaking change and discover the impact through consumer failures, or preserve an old API indefinitely because the risk is unknown. Libraries need to evolve, and their producers need evidence that helps them do so intentionally.
We built Quasar to index symbol definitions and references across Netflix repositories. For library producers, that shared index helps answer two questions:

What changed in the library’s public API?
Which repositories use the exact symbols that changed?

The first identifies a potentially incompatible change. The second estimates its observed blast radius. Together, they turn a generic compatibility warning into evidence a producer can act on before merging or releasing.
From API Changes to Consumer Impact
Existing techniques each see a different part of the problem. Binary and source compatibility tools identify contract changes, but cannot tell who uses the changed API. Dependency graphs show declared reach, but cannot prove that code calls a particular method. Text search may miss overloads, inheritance, or the artifact version behind a call. Consumer builds provide strong validation, but running them across the fleet is expensive.
Quasar builds on SCIP, an open interchange format for semantic code intelligence. Language-specific indexers encode definitions, references, and relationships using stable symbol identifiers. Quasar retains API definitions for library versions and commits alongside references from consumer repositories. That shared identity lets it connect an API change in one repository to exact usages elsewhere, even when those repositories were indexed independently.

On each enrolled CI build, language-specific indexers submit SCIP indexes to Quasar’s ingestion service. It writes API definitions and consumer references as Parquet in Amazon S3, retaining the symbol identity, dependency version, and source location needed to investigate a change.
During pull-request review, Quasar compares indexed base and head definitions and counts direct consumer references with Amazon Athena. Quasar exposes those findings through its REST and GraphQL APIs and MCP server; follow-up usage queries provide dependency-version breakdowns and source locations. A separate compatibility-impact assessment can also follow implementations and their callers when a producer supplies a changed JVM symbol.
Consider this simplified API change:
public interface Client {
- Result getLegacyValue(Request request);
+ Result getValue(Request request, Options options);
}
For a detailed compatibility-impact assessment of this removal, a producer-side tool supplies the old method descriptor. Quasar constructs its canonical symbol identity. This abridged excerpt from the direct-reference portion of Quasar’s Amazon Athena query shows the essential match:
SELECT c.change_id, 'DIRECT_REFERENCE' AS evidence_kind,
       r.scm_type, r.org, r.repo, r.dep_version, r.file_path
FROM requested_changes c
JOIN quasar.symbol_refs r
  ON r.symbol_canonical = c.target_canonical
requested_changes contains the API changes submitted by the producer. The SQL excerpt finds repositories that call the removed method. Quasar also checks implementations and calls through them, so it can count each affected repository once. It returns sample dependency versions and file locations to help investigate the result.
For the Client change, this tells the producer which repositories still use getLegacyValue, which versions they use, and where some of those calls occur. That helps the producer decide whether to coordinate a migration before removing the method.
Bringing the Analysis Before Release
Version-to-version comparison is valuable when planning an upgrade or writing a migration guide. Producers benefit even more when feedback arrives during code review.
For pull-request analysis, Quasar stores API definition snapshots keyed by commit. Given a base and head commit, it classifies symbols as added, removed, or signature-modified. Removals and modifications then become candidates for consumer-impact analysis.
An incompatible change is not automatically a high-risk change. Quasar reports the observed impact so the producer can decide what to do; it does not enforce a release policy. “No references observed” means only that Quasar found none in the indexed population. Reflection, configuration, dynamic loading, stale branches, or incomplete indexing can hide consumers. The result needs to show whether the requested commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated.
Pull-request review requires indexed snapshots for the exact base and head commits. If either is unavailable, Quasar reports that it cannot compare them; it does not substitute a default-branch snapshot. This keeps a missing comparison from looking like a clean API diff.
Return to our Client change. This illustrative report brings together signals available through Quasar's API comparison, consumer-usage queries, and library-level criticality. It is not a literal response from one API:
{
  "change": "REMOVED",
  "symbol": "Client#getLegacyValue(Request)",
  "affectedRepositories": 137,
  "versionDistribution": [
    { "version": "4.2.1", "repositories": 86 },
    { "version": "4.1.7", "repositories": 38 },
    { "version": "3.9.4", "repositories": 13 }
  ],
  "sampleConsumerLocations": [
    {
      "repository": "checkout-service",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/checkout/CheckoutClient.java",
      "lines": [84, 129]
    },
    {
      "repository": "client-wrapper",
      "filePath": "src/main/java/com/example/client/ClientAdapter.java",
      "lines": [57]
    }
  ],
  "libraryCriticality": {
    "tier": 1,
    "basis": "highest-tier downstream application"
  },
  "comparison": {
    "baseShaFound": true,
    "headShaFound": true
  }
}An impact report shows 137 affected repositories distributed across library versions 4.2.1, 4.1.7, and 3.9.4.
The repository count is symbol-specific: in this example, 137 indexed repositories refer to the removed method. The version distribution reveals a dominant cohort on 4.2.1 and a smaller long tail still on 3.9.4. A producer can inspect affected repositories and retrieve indexed file paths, with line numbers where the index provides them. The JSON shows only two sample locations to keep the example readable. The filePath and lines shape mirrors Quasar's query contract. The tier is broader context about the library, inherited from its highest-criticality downstream application; it does not imply that all 137 callers are Tier 1.
Together, those signals change the producer’s plan. Instead of merging the removal and waiting for failures, the producer can retain and deprecate the old method, publish a migration path, coordinate a broader migration, and track the long-tail versions before removal. File paths and available line numbers turn that scope into a concrete work list for engineers or coding agents. The same API diff paired with weak or stale evidence would lead to a different action: refresh the indexes before deciding. The value is not merely detecting the removal; it is choosing a proportionate next step.
A pre-release workflow enriches API changes with consumer impact and evidence quality before the producer decides how to proceed
A Polyglot Foundation with SCIP
The shared SCIP format also lets Quasar index several language ecosystems. Each language indexer resolves its own code, while Quasar can use the resulting symbol identities to find references across repositories.
Conceptually, client-lib indexes Client#getLegacyValue(Request) as a definition, while checkout-service indexes a reference to the same symbol. Quasar can then connect the library API to its consumer across repositories.
Language-specific indexers emit SCIP definitions, references, and relationships into Quasar’s shared semantic graph.
Relationships are especially useful when generated code separates the API a producer owns from the symbols consumers invoke. For example, Quasar can trace a Protobuf definition through its generated Java members to the repositories that use them, even when consumer code never names the .proto element.
SCIP records symbols and their references; it does not determine whether an API change violates an ecosystem’s compatibility rules. Today, Quasar compares indexed JVM and Protobuf API definitions and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java to find affected repositories. A separate JVM compatibility-impact path uses breaks identified by a producer-side tool to query affected repositories. Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust support usage queries, but Quasar does not yet assess their breaking API changes.
Moving Risk Assessment Earlier
Today, Quasar surfaces API-change findings on pull requests, including observed consumer counts and confidence. Producers can use its other queries to inspect dependency versions and source locations, with library criticality as broader context. Together, those signals support a decision before merge.
We want to move that context earlier. An agent writing library code should recognize when it is changing a public symbol and consult Quasar before the change becomes a pull request. Quasar’s APIs and Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration provide an access path, but access alone does not create awareness. The coding workflow must also recognize public API edits so the agent knows when to query impact and when to involve the producer.
Today Quasar assesses risk on a pull request. The future workflow gives agents consumer-impact context while they write code, before the pull request is opened.
Earlier guidance will not replace pull-request analysis. The PR assessment will still verify the concrete diff and catch changes that were not recognized during coding. Coverage, freshness, ambiguity, unsupported platforms, and truncation must travel through both checks in machine-readable form. An agent should not turn “no observed usages in the available index” into “safe to remove.”
Today, agents can query Quasar through MCP when prompted. We are working toward making that context part of the coding workflow, then using identified call sites to prepare migration changes. Quasar supplies semantic evidence, an agent reduces migration toil, and the library producer remains responsible for API and release decisions.
What We Learned
Building this workflow led us to four practical lessons.

Separate compatibility from reach. A removed method can break the API contract even when Quasar finds no callers. A list of affected repositories and their library versions shows the migration work ahead. Producers need both signals to choose a release path.
Make the evidence inspectable. A repository count is more useful with sample call sites and a version breakdown. The result also needs to show which commits were indexed, how fresh the consumer indexes are, and whether evidence was truncated. Otherwise, “no usage found” can be mistaken for proof that nobody is affected.
Keep usage and compatibility separate across languages. SCIP lets Quasar find symbol references in several ecosystems. Deciding whether an API change is breaking requires compatibility rules or a trusted producer-side signal for that ecosystem.
Bring evidence to the producer while choices are open. Pull-request findings can prompt a producer to retain an API, publish a migration path, or coordinate consumers before merge. Moving the same evidence into the coding workflow could shape the edit earlier. After release, it still helps locate consumers that need to migrate.

Today, Quasar indexes JVM, Go, Python, JavaScript/TypeScript, and Rust code for cross-repository usage analysis. It compares JVM APIs and traces Protobuf changes through generated Java. Producers can review change findings through Quasar’s REST and GraphQL APIs or its MCP server, then investigate affected repositories and call sites. We are extending this foundation toward more ecosystem-specific compatibility checks, deeper code-review integration, and agent-assisted consumer migrations that keep release approval with the producer.
Quasar is internal to Netflix, but the pattern is portable: index code semantically, retain API definitions, compare them at the point of change, query affected consumers, and report the quality of the evidence. Library producers need more than a compatibility verdict. They need to know who may be affected and have enough time to act before release.
A huge thank you to the Java Platform team at Netflix. Their expertise, collaboration, and support made this work possible
Related Talks

From Lag to Lightning: Transforming Dependency Update Timelines explores how Netflix shortened dependency-update timelines.
Netflix’s Journey to Confident Automated Code Changes discusses building confidence in automated changes at scale.
